title: Bardia National Park Safari Guide
meta_description: Bardia National Park safari guide: tigers, river dolphins, jeep and walking safaris, rafting on the Karnali, Tharu villages, seasons, fees and getting there.
summary: Bardia is Nepal's largest lowland national park, 968 km² of sal forest, grassland and Karnali river channels, and one of the best places in Asia to look for wild tigers. Fly to Nepalgunj, drive 90 km to Thakurdwara, and give it three or four nights: a full-day jeep safari, a day on foot and a float on the river.

sections.heading: Why Bardia
paras: Nepalis who work in wildlife tend to speak about Bardia with a particular fondness. It is the largest national park in the Terai, 968 km², and it protects the country where the Karnali, Nepal's longest river, breaks out of the hills at Chisapani and spreads into braided channels across the plain. To the east the park takes in the Babai river valley. Between them lie sal forest, riverine woodland and phanta, the open grasslands where deer gather and tigers hunt.

The park began as the Royal Karnali Wildlife Reserve in 1976 and became a national park in 1988. A buffer zone around it, where villages share in park income, was added in 1996. Over the past two decades Bardia has been one of the success stories of Nepal's tiger conservation: national tiger surveys have shown its population rising strongly, and it now holds one of the largest tiger populations of any park in the country.

What makes Bardia different from Chitwan is quiet. Chitwan has many more lodges, roads and visitors. Bardia's lodges are concentrated in one village, Thakurdwara, beside the park headquarters, and on a full-day drive you may see only two or three other jeeps. Walking safaris are normal here, and the guides who lead them are some of the most experienced trackers in Nepal.

sections.heading: Getting there and where to stay
paras: The gateway is Nepalgunj, a busy border city on the plain with an airport served by several daily flights from Kathmandu, about one hour. From Nepalgunj Airport it is about 90 km to Thakurdwara, 2 to 2.5 hours by car: west along the East–West Highway to Kohalpur, on to Ambassa, then north on a country road through Tharu villages. By road from Kathmandu the trip is 12 to 14 hours, and from Chitwan about 8 to 9 hours, a long but straightforward drive on the highway.

Almost all accommodation is in Thakurdwara and the villages beside it, from family-run guesthouses with garden huts to full-board safari lodges. Tiger Tops Karnali Lodge is the best-known of the established lodges. Some homestays in nearby villages, such as the community homestay at Dalla, let you stay with Tharu families. Whatever you choose, book the lodge's own guides or an experienced private naturalist; the quality of your guide shapes your safari more than the room.

sections.heading: Ways to see the park
paras: All activities inside the park go with licensed nature guides. Most visitors combine two or three of the options below over three or four days. A first-timer's ideal mix is one full day by jeep, one morning on foot, and an afternoon on the river.

On walking safaris you go with two licensed guides and follow their rules exactly: stay close, stay quiet, never run.
Bring binoculars; many sightings in Bardia are at a distance across a river channel.

sections.heading: Tigers: how the search works
paras: Bardia's tigers are wild and the park is large, so a sighting is never guaranteed. Guides improve your chances by working with the heat. In spring, from March to May, tigers come to the river channels in the middle of the day to drink and cool off, and the best tactic is to sit quietly on a high bank overlooking a crossing for hours at a time. It feels slow. It is how most tigers are seen here.

Guides also read the forest. A spotted deer's sharp alarm call, a langur barking from a treetop, fresh pugmarks on wet sand, scratch marks on a tree at shoulder height: each tells them where a tiger has been and sometimes where it is. On foot you learn to read these signs yourself, and even without a sighting the day feels like detective work.

Respect matters. Never ask a driver to leave the track, never crowd an animal, and never play calls to attract it. The park and buffer-zone communities live alongside tigers, and there are conflicts when tigers take livestock or, rarely, people. Your visit supports the communities through park fees and local jobs, which is part of why tiger numbers have grown.

sections.heading: River life: dolphins, crocodiles and rafting
paras: The Karnali and its Geruwa channel make Bardia a river park as much as a forest park. Mugger crocodiles bask on sandbanks, and the critically endangered gharial, a slender-snouted fish-eating crocodile, has been released into the park's rivers to rebuild its numbers. The crocodile breeding centre at the park headquarters in Thakurdwara is worth a short visit.

The Karnali is also one of the last rivers in Nepal where the Gangetic river dolphin survives. The population is very small, and dolphins are seen most often in deep pools of the Karnali near Chisapani and in the Geruwa in the cooler months. A sighting is a grey back and a puff of breath, gone in a second. A gentle raft float on the Geruwa is the easiest way to look for them, and for river birds such as ospreys, kingfishers and river lapwings.

For white water, the Karnali is one of Nepal's great rafting rivers. Multi-day expeditions start in the hills far upstream and run through deep gorges and big rapids before finishing near Chisapani, at the edge of the park. Some travellers end such a trip with a few days in Bardia. Rafting companies in Kathmandu run these trips in the dry seasons; ask us if you want to combine the two.

sections.heading: The Tharu and the Sonaha of Bardia
paras: The villages around the park are mostly Tharu, the people of the Terai who lived in these forests long before the parks were drawn. In Bardia they are mainly Dangaura Tharu, whose families once lived in large longhouses shared by several generations. Walls are made of mud and straw over a frame of wood, and grain is stored in tall bins built into the house. You may be offered rice, river fish, snails cooked with spices, and dhikri, steamed rolls of rice flour.

Look out also for the Sonaha, a small community who live along the Karnali and have traditionally fished and panned the river sand for gold. Their lives are closely tied to the river, and the park's rules have changed how they work. Ask your guide to introduce you if you are visiting a riverside village.

The biggest Tharu festival is Maghi, the Tharu new year in mid-January, with feasting, dancing and family gatherings. Around Dashain in autumn, village groups dance the sakhiya in circles. A homestay night or a cooking visit is the best way to understand how people live beside a tiger park.

sections.heading: Seasons, fees and rules
paras: October and November are green, cool and clear. December and January bring cold, foggy mornings on the plain, pleasant afternoons and fewer animals at the rivers. February to May is the best time for tigers: villagers are allowed to cut thatch grass in the park for a short period in winter, which opens up the phanta, and as the heat builds animals stay near water. May afternoons can pass 40 °C. From mid-June to September the monsoon floods tracks and most jungle activities stop.

Foreign visitors pay a park entry fee per day, about NPR 1,500 plus VAT at the time of writing. Since April 2023 Nepal requires foreign visitors in national parks to go with a licensed guide, and in Bardia all activities inside the park already require one. Fees and rules change, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How many days do I need in Bardia National Park?
faqs.a: Three nights is the minimum we suggest, four is better. That gives you one full-day jeep safari, a walking safari, a river float and time in a Tharu village, with a spare half day for a second try at a tiger. Because the journey to Bardia takes most of a day each way, shorter visits rarely feel worth it.

faqs.q: Is Bardia better than Chitwan for tigers?
faqs.a: Many guides think so. Bardia has had strong tiger numbers in recent national surveys, far fewer vehicles, and a tradition of walking safaris and long riverbank watches that suit tiger spotting. Chitwan is easier to reach and has more rhinos and lodges. If tigers are your priority and you have time, choose Bardia.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Bardia?
faqs.a: February to May for tigers and other large mammals, because grass is short and animals come to the rivers in the heat. October and November are the most comfortable months, green and clear. December and January are foggy at dawn. Avoid mid-June to September, when the monsoon closes most of the park.

faqs.q: How do I get from Kathmandu to Bardia?
faqs.a: Fly from Kathmandu to Nepalgunj, about an hour, then drive about 90 km to Thakurdwara, which takes 2 to 2.5 hours. By road the whole way is 12 to 14 hours. From Chitwan or Lumbini you can drive west along the East–West Highway in a long day.

faqs.q: Are walking safaris in Bardia dangerous?
faqs.a: There is real risk, as with any walk among tigers, rhinos and wild elephants, but it is managed. Walks are led by two licensed guides, groups are small, and the rules are strict: keep close, keep quiet, never run. Serious incidents involving visitors are rare. If you are not comfortable, choose a jeep day instead.

faqs.q: Can I see river dolphins in Bardia?
faqs.a: Possibly. The Karnali and its Geruwa channel hold one of Nepal's last populations of the endangered Gangetic river dolphin. They are seen most often in deep pools near Chisapani and in the cooler months, usually as a brief roll at the surface. A raft float on the Geruwa gives you a reasonable chance.

faqs.q: What does the Bardia park entry fee cost?
faqs.a: At the time of writing foreigners pay about NPR 1,500 plus VAT per day, with lower rates for SAARC nationals and Nepalis. The fee is paid at the park office in Thakurdwara, usually by your lodge or guide. Fees change, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Where should I stay in Bardia?
faqs.a: In Thakurdwara, next to the park headquarters, where nearly all lodges are. Options run from simple family guesthouses to full-board lodges such as Tiger Tops Karnali Lodge. Tharu homestays in nearby villages, such as Dalla, give a cultural stay. Pick the lodge with the best guides, not the biggest pool.

Yes, for children old enough to sit quietly in a jeep for a few hours. The crocodile breeding centre, Tharu village visits and river floats suit families well. Walking safaris have age limits set by guides and the park. In spring heat, plan activities for early morning and late afternoon.
